passage: I'm Bhupen, and I saw my sister Sabina roll her eyes when Ma asked her to fold the clothes. Ma's face went tight. “What was that?” “Nothing.” I couldn't tell if Sabina was bored, tired from school, or still angry about the argument earlier. Ma took a breath. “Sabina, you seem fed up. What's up?” Sabina sat down on the bed. “I've folded the clothes three times this week and Bhupen never does.” Ma nodded. “Fair. Bhupen, you do it tomorrow.” I sulked, but it was fair.

qa.q: What did Ma ask Sabina to fold?
qa.a: She asked her to fold the clothes.

qa.q: What was Sabina probably feeling behind the eye-roll, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: Fed up, because she felt the chore was unfair, as she said she had folded the clothes three times and Bhupen never does. It could also have been tiredness or boredom, as Bhupen guessed.

qa.q: How did Ma's question open a better talk?
qa.a: She named that Sabina seemed fed up and asked what was up, instead of arguing about the eye-roll. That let the real complaint come out.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel about the outcome?
qa.a: He sulked, but he admits it was fair, so he seems to feel a bit caught out and also accepts it. 😅

grounding: An eye-roll signals annoyance and a calm question opens a better talk.

passage:
Monday: when Ms Anjali reminded the class about the spelling test, Elizabeth rolled her eyes. Ms Anjali said nothing but noticed.
Wednesday: Elizabeth rolled her eyes again. After class Ms Anjali said calmly, “I noticed the eye-roll. What's going on?” Elizabeth shrugged. “The words are too easy. I finish first and wait.” Ms Anjali nodded. “Thank you for telling me.”
Friday: Ms Anjali handed Elizabeth an extra list of long words. There was no eye-roll. Elizabeth said, “Can I have the hardest one first?”

qa.q: On which day did Ms Anjali ask Elizabeth what was going on?
qa.a: She asked on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth probably feeling when she rolled her eyes on Monday, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably bored, since she later said the words were too easy and she finishes first and waits. It could also have been mild annoyance at being reminded.

qa.q: How did Ms Anjali's approach work better than scolding?
qa.a: She calmly asked what was going on, so Elizabeth explained, and the answer led to an extra list that solved the boredom.

qa.q: How might Ms Anjali have felt when she first saw the eye-roll?
qa.a: Possibly a little stung or puzzled, but she said nothing and waited to ask privately. That gave her a real answer instead of an argument.

grounding: An eye-roll signals boredom or annoyance; calmly asking what is wrong opens a better conversation.

passage: Damini, you think your papa never rolled his eyes? Let me, your old Dada Madhav, tell you. When he was nine, I asked him every evening to fetch the milk. One day he rolled his eyes so hard I thought they'd stick. I was about to shout. Then I remembered my own father shouting, and how I'd go silent and stew. So I sat down on the step and asked, “What's wrong with the milk?” He was quiet. Then it came out: the bigger boys teased him at the dairy. That same evening we walked there together, and after that he went with his cousin. The eye-rolling stopped soon after.

qa.q: What did Madhav ask his son to fetch every evening?
qa.a: He asked him to fetch the milk.

qa.q: What was the boy feeling behind his eye-roll?
qa.a: It looked like annoyance, but the boy was probably embarrassed and scared of the bigger boys who teased him at the dairy.

qa.q: What choice did Madhav make instead of shouting, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He sat down and calmly asked what was wrong, which let his son explain the teasing so they could fix the real problem.

qa.q: How might the boy have felt when his father walked with him to the dairy?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and protected, knowing his father had taken the teasing seriously.

grounding: Shows a child's eye-roll as a way to avoid a spoken argument, and a parent's calm question opening a better talk.

passage: The fan had stopped working, the last period was dragging, and the corridor outside was loud with another class's practice. Salma Ma'am asked Karthik to rewrite his paragraph neatly. Karthik rolled his eyes, slowly, all the way up to the ceiling. A few kids went “Ooooh.” Salma felt the heat rise in her own face. Instead of snapping, she walked over and spoke under the noise. “That eye-roll said something. What is it?” Karthik scowled at his notebook. “My hand hurts. I already wrote it twice. And it's so hot.” She looked at his cramped, sweaty writing. “Fair. Rewrite just the first three lines. Water first.”

qa.q: How many lines did Salma Ma'am ask Karthik to rewrite in the end?
qa.a: She asked him to rewrite just the first three lines.

qa.q: What was Karthik most likely feeling when he rolled his eyes?
qa.a: It most likely expressed frustration and tiredness, since his hand hurt, he'd written it twice and the room was hot, rather than pure disrespect.

qa.q: Why did asking about the eye-roll work better than snapping?
qa.a: Asking calmly under the noise let Karthik say what was wrong, so Salma could adjust the task instead of starting a power struggle.

qa.q: What was it like for Salma when the class went “Ooooh”?
qa.a: She felt her face heat up, as if her authority was being tested, which made staying calm harder.

grounding: Shows a teacher reading a child's eye-roll as annoyance, and calmly asking what was wrong to open a better talk.

passage: In their flat in Nagpur, Urmila was helping her younger sister Sonali pack her bag for the school trip. “Take the jacket. It gets cold on the bus.” Sonali rolled her eyes and zipped the bag shut. Urmila's first thought was, Fine, freeze then. She almost said it. Instead she sat on the bed. “You rolled your eyes. Is it the jacket, or me?” Sonali picked at the zip. “It's the jacket. It's the old pink one. Everyone will laugh.” “Ah.” Urmila went to her cupboard and held out her own grey hoodie. “Borrow this?” Sonali grinned and unzipped the bag.

qa.q: Where was Sonali going?
qa.a: Sonali was going on the school trip.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when Sonali rolled her eyes?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and brushed off, nearly snapping, before choosing to ask instead.

qa.q: What did asking reveal that the eye-roll hid?
qa.a: It showed Sonali was embarrassed about the old pink jacket, not rejecting her sister's advice, so the hoodie solved it.

qa.q: What was the jacket worry like for Sonali?
qa.a: Sonali was afraid others would laugh at the old pink jacket, and rolling her eyes was easier than saying so.

grounding: Shows an older sibling reading an eye-roll as dismissal, and a calm question revealing embarrassment underneath.

passage:
"Once more, Zainab. Write the seven times table again."
Zainab rolled her eyes to the ceiling and let out a long breath.
"I saw that," said Rukmini Ma'am.
"Saw what?"
"The eyes. Tell me what's wrong, in words."
"Nothing."
"Nothing doesn't roll its eyes."
Zainab's pen tapped the table. "It's the third time today. I know it already. And my hand hurts from school."
"Ah. So you're bored and tired, not being rude to me?"
"…Mostly."
Rukmini Ma'am smiled. "Fair. Say it aloud to me instead, fast as you can. Get it right and there's no more writing."
"Seven, fourteen, twenty-one…"

qa.q: Which times table was Zainab asked to write again?
qa.a: The seven times table.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling behind her eye roll?
qa.a: She felt bored and annoyed at writing the same table a third time, and tired from a sore hand; the roll let her show it without starting an argument.

qa.q: Which choice turned the eye roll into a better talk?
qa.a: Rukmini Ma'am calmly asked what was wrong in words instead of scolding, then changed the task to saying it aloud.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Ma'am feel when Zainab says "…Mostly"?
qa.a: She seems amused and understanding 🙂, taking the honest answer instead of treating the eye roll as an insult.

grounding: It shows a child rolling her eyes at a tutor out of boredom and annoyance, and a calm question opening a better talk than a scolding.
